title: Idioms describing people
subtitle: a heart of gold, a head like a sieve
summary: Use English idioms to describe what people are like - their kindness, their common sense, how odd they are, and who is who in the classroom.

left.label: Positive
examples: She has a **heart of gold**. [very kind, generous]
He's **as good as gold**. [helpful, well-behaved - used generally for children]
Her **heart's in the right place**. [she is a good and kind person even if she doesn't always seem so]

right.label: Negative
examples: She's **as hard as nails**. [no sympathy for others]
He's such an **awkward customer**. [a difficult person to deal with]

lesson.heading: Difficult people
lesson.text: Two very common idioms describe someone who annoys everyone. Note that **a pain in the neck** always takes *the*, while **get on someone's nerves** always takes a possessive.

examples.text: She's **a pain in the neck**. Nobody likes her.
My little brother really **gets on my nerves** when I'm trying to work.

lesson.heading: Idioms based on 'head'
rows: to have your head screwed on
to have a head for heights
to have a head like a sieve
to have a good head for figures
to have your head in the clouds
to be head and shoulders above someone
to bury your head in the sand
refuse to think about a difficult situation
stay calm in a difficult situation
lesson.note: Learning idioms in groups round a key word - gold, heart, head - makes them much easier to remember.

lesson.heading: How people relate to the social norm
lesson.text: These idioms place someone on a scale from completely normal to completely mad.

examples.text: He's **gone round the bend**, if you ask me.

examples.note: very normal, neither left- nor right-wing

lesson.heading: Who's who in the class
rows: the one who gets the best marks
someone who thinks they know everything
someone with a high opinion of themselves
lesson.note: Know-all, big-head and lazy-bones are used about people outside the classroom too.

lesson.text: *As good as gold* is used mainly about children; *a heart of gold* is used about anyone who is very kind.

exercises.prompt: She does a lot of voluntary work; she has a heart ___.
exercises.explanation: To have a heart of gold = to be very kind and generous.

exercises.prompt: Don't expect any sympathy from the boss; she's as hard ___.
exercises.explanation: As hard as nails = having no sympathy for other people.

exercises.prompt: I'm sure Ahmed will help you; he's as good ___.
exercises.explanation: As good as gold = helpful and well-behaved.

exercises.prompt: Although Florian sometimes seems bad-tempered, his heart is ___.
exercises.explanation: If someone's heart is in the right place, they are kind even though they may not seem so.

exercises.prompt: I don't think you'll like him; he's a nasty ___.
exercises.explanation: A nasty piece of work = a thoroughly unpleasant person.

exercises.prompt: Match each classroom character with the description.

pairs.left: an irritating person who thinks they know everything
someone who thinks they are the best and says so
the one who gets the best marks
a person who is very lazy

exercises.prompt: I'd better write it in my notebook. I have a head like ___.
exercises.explanation: To have a head like a sieve = to have a very bad memory.

exercises.prompt: Ask Martha to check those sums. She has a good head for ___.
exercises.explanation: A good head for figures = being good at maths.

exercises.prompt: Don't ask me to go up that tower. I'm afraid I don't have a head for ___.
exercises.explanation: To have a head for heights = not to suffer from vertigo.

exercises.prompt: The problem won't go away, so there's no point ___.
options: burying your head in the sand
being head and shoulders above the rest
exercises.explanation: To bury your head in the sand = to refuse to think about a difficult situation.

exercises.prompt: Even when everyone around him is panicking, Raul always ___.
options: has his head in the clouds
has a head like a sieve
exercises.explanation: To keep your head = to stay calm in a difficult situation.

exercises.prompt: Which part of the body completes each idiom?

items.text: My brother really gets on my ___
That noise is a pain in ___
He has his ___ in the clouds

exercises.statement: If your politics are *middle-of-the-road*, you have very radical, left-wing ideas.
exercises.explanation: Middle-of-the-road means very normal, with no radical ideas - neither left- nor right-wing.

exercises.answer: Max is head and shoulders above everyone else in the class.
exercises.explanation: To be head and shoulders above someone = to be much better than them.
